agenda

/uh-JEN-duh/ — stress on JEN · noun

Hear It

What It Means

An agenda is a list of items or topics to be discussed or accomplished, such as during a meeting or over the course of a day.

The first item on the meeting's agenda was the leaking roof.

Example

The principal walks into the staff meeting with a printed agenda: discuss the science lab renovation, review the new attendance policy, approve the field trip budget. She presents each item in order and keeps the group focused on completing every topic before dismissal.

Agenda is more precise than "list" or "plan" because it names a structured list of topics or items to be addressed in a meeting or organized event. A plain "list" is too vague; agenda suggests purpose, order, and formal discussion in a specific context.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

list: A list is the barest way of writing things down — items set one after another, with no occasion attached and nothing decided about order or purpose. An agenda is a list with a job: it names the topics a meeting will take up, usually in the order the group will discuss them.

plan: A plan is a thought-out way of getting something done — the how, the strategy behind an effort. An agenda never explains how anything will be accomplished; it only sets out what a meeting will deal with, item by item. A plan carries method; an agenda carries topics.

itinerary: An itinerary is the schedule of a journey — where you will be and when, stop by stop. An agenda organizes a discussion rather than a trip: it lists the topics a meeting will cover. Use itinerary for travel days, agenda for meeting rooms.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

improvisation: doing things unplanned, in the moment

spontaneity: acting freely without any set plan

Where it sits · how detailed and fixed the plan is

chaos → rough outline → agenda → rigid schedule

chaos vs. agenda: Chaos is the far weak end of the scale from agenda: chaos means no plan whatsoever, while an agenda lays out exactly what will be discussed or done.

rough outline vs. agenda: A rough outline is weaker than an agenda — it sketches only the general shape of a plan, while an agenda lists each specific item to be covered.

rigid schedule vs. agenda: A rigid schedule is stronger than an agenda: an agenda lists what will happen, but a rigid schedule locks every item to an exact time and allows no changes.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ag-: to do, drive, set in motion (Latin agere) (Latin)

Suffix — -enda: things that must be (done) — a gerundive ending (Latin)

Put it together: In Latin, agenda literally means 'things that must be done' — ag- ('to do') plus the gerundive ending -enda ('must be...'). An agenda is still exactly that: the list of things to be done or discussed.

Use the root in a new word: agent: The actor's agent phoned during dinner with news about the audition.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Use agenda when referring to a structured list of topics for a meeting or organized activity. For a personal to-do list, shopping list, or casual checklist, list or plan fits better. For a detailed timetable of a journey, itinerary is more precise.
